title: The Willow-Wren and the Bear
paragraphs: One summer the bear and the wolf were walking in the forest when the bear heard a bird singing so beautifully that he said, “Brother wolf, what kind of bird sings so well?” “That is the King of the birds,” said the wolf, “and we must bow down to him.” In fact the bird was the willow-wren. “If that’s so,” said the bear, “I’d very much like to see his royal palace. Come, take me there.” “It isn’t done as simply as you seem to think,” said the wolf. “You have to wait until the Queen arrives.” Soon afterward the Queen came with some food in her beak, and the lord King came too, and they began to feed their young. The bear wanted to go in at once, but the wolf held him back by the sleeve and said, “No, you must wait until the lord and lady Queen have gone away again.” So they noted the hole where the nest lay and trotted off. The bear, however, couldn’t rest until he had seen the royal palace, and after a short while he went back. The King and Queen had just flown out, so he peeked in and saw five or six young ones lying there. “Is this the royal palace?” cried the bear. “What a wretched palace! And you aren’t King’s children, you’re disreputable brats!” When the young wrens heard this, they were furiously angry and screamed, “No, we are not! Our parents are honest people! Bear, you’ll pay for that!”

The bear and the wolf grew uneasy, turned back and went into their dens. The young willow-wrens, though, kept on crying and screaming, and when their parents came again with food they said, “We won’t so much as touch a fly’s leg, not even if we’re starving, until you have settled whether we are respectable children or not. The bear has been here and insulted us!” Then the old King said, “Calm down, he will be punished.” He flew straight off with the Queen to the bear’s cave and called in, “Old Growler, why have you insulted my children? You will suffer for it. We will punish you with a bloody war.” So war was declared on the Bear, and all the four-footed animals were called up to fight in it: oxen, asses, cows, deer, and every other animal the earth held. And the willow-wren called up everything that flew in the air, not only birds large and small, but midges too, and hornets, bees and flies.

When the day of the war drew near, the willow-wren sent out scouts to find out who would command the enemy. The gnat, the sneakiest of them all, flew into the forest where the enemy had gathered and hid under a leaf on the very tree where the password was to be given out. There stood the bear. He called the fox over and said, “Fox, you’re the cleverest animal there is. You’ll be our general and lead us.” “Very well,” said the fox, “but what signal should we agree on?” Nobody had an answer, so the fox said, “I have a fine long bushy tail that looks almost like a plume of red feathers. When I hold my tail up high, things are going well, and you should charge. But if I let it hang down, run for your lives.” Once the gnat had heard this, she flew back and told the willow-wren everything, down to the smallest detail. At daybreak, when the battle was about to begin, all the four-footed animals came racing up so noisily that the ground shook. The willow-wren and his army came flying through the air as well, humming and whirring and swarming so loudly that everyone grew uneasy and afraid, and the two sides advanced on each other. But the willow-wren sent the hornet down with orders to settle under the fox’s tail and sting with all his strength. At the first sting the fox flinched and lifted one leg in pain, but he bore it and kept his tail high in the air. At the second sting he had to lower it for a moment. At the third he could stand it no longer: he screamed and tucked his tail between his legs. When the animals saw that, they thought everything was lost and fled, each to his own hole, and the birds won the battle.

Then the King and Queen flew home to their children and called out, “Children, be glad! Eat and drink as much as you like. We’ve won the battle!” But the young wrens said, “We won’t eat yet. First the bear has to come to the nest, beg our pardon and say that we are honorable children. Only then will we eat.” So the willow-wren flew to the bear’s hole and shouted, “Growler, you must come to the nest, to my children, and beg their pardon, or every rib in your body will be broken.” The bear crept over, terrified, and begged their pardon. Only then were the young wrens satisfied. They sat down together, ate and drank, and made merry until late into the night.
